title: What training does the EU Chemical Agents Directive require for workers?
description: What Article 8 of Directive 98/24/EC requires for worker information and training on hazardous chemical agents, linked to risk assessment and safety drills.
shortAnswer: The EU Chemical Agents Directive (Council Directive 98/24/EC) requires employers to give workers and their representatives the risk assessment data, information on the hazardous chemical agents present, training on precautions and actions to protect themselves and others, and access to supplier safety data sheets. Under Article 8, the depth of training must match the risk assessment, ranging from oral communication to individual instruction backed by written information, and must be updated when circumstances change.
keyTakeaways: Article 8 of Directive 98/24/EC sets four information and training elements: risk assessment data, agent information, training on precautions and actions, and access to safety data sheets.
The form of training is scaled to the Article 4 risk assessment, from oral communication up to individual instruction and training supported by written information.
Article 7 separately requires emergency action plans that include relevant safety drills performed at regular intervals.
The directive was amended in 2014 to align with the CLP Regulation and REACH, and in 2024 to add a binding limit value for diisocyanates with a transitional value until December 31, 2028.
Asbestos and carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances have their own, stricter directives that apply on top of this one.
jurisdiction: European Union (applied through each Member State's national law)
regulator: National labor inspectorates enforce the transposing laws; the European Commission monitors transposition; the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work (EU-OSHA) publishes guidance
appliesTo: Employers in any sector where hazardous chemical agents are or may be present at the workplace
Workers exposed or potentially exposed to hazardous chemical agents, including maintenance staff
Workers' representatives with a safety and health role
Workers assigned to emergency response, repair, and first aid roles for chemical incidents

sections.heading: What is the EU Chemical Agents Directive?

blocks.text: The Chemical Agents Directive is [Council Directive 98/24/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31998L0024) of April 7, 1998, the European Union's baseline law on protecting workers from risks caused by chemical agents at work. It is the fourteenth individual directive under the [OSH Framework Directive](/regulations/eu-osh-framework-directive-training), so the Framework Directive's general training duty in Article 12 still applies and Article 8 of the Chemical Agents Directive adds chemical specific content on top.

Article 1(2) says the requirements apply "where hazardous chemical agents are present or may be present at the workplace". After the 2014 amendment, a hazardous chemical agent is defined in Article 2(b) by reference to the hazard classes in the Classification, Labelling and Packaging (CLP) Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008, whether or not the agent is actually classified under that Regulation. That definition captures process fumes, by-products, and waste, not only purchased products.

Member States had to transpose the directive by May 5, 2001 (Article 14). As at November 2026, the [consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:01998L0024-20240408) reflects four amending acts: Directive 2007/30/EC, Directive 2014/27/EU, Regulation (EU) 2019/1243, and Directive (EU) 2024/869.

sections.heading: What does Article 8 require employers to provide?

blocks.text: Article 8(1) requires the employer to ensure that workers and/or their representatives receive four things. It applies "without prejudice to Articles 10 and 12 of Directive 89/391/EEC", meaning the Framework Directive's general information and training duties continue in parallel.

items: **Risk assessment data:** the data obtained under Article 4, with further information whenever a major alteration at the workplace changes that data.
**Agent information:** the identity of the hazardous chemical agents present, their risks to safety and health, relevant occupational exposure limit values, and other legislative provisions.
**Training and information on precautions:** the appropriate precautions and actions workers must take to safeguard themselves and other workers.
**Safety data sheets:** access to any safety data sheet provided by the supplier under Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH), as substituted by Directive 2014/27/EU.

blocks.text: Article 8(1) then sets two quality conditions. The information must be "provided in a manner appropriate to the outcome of the risk assessment", which "may vary from oral communication to individual instruction and training supported by information in writing, depending on the nature and degree of the risk". It must also be "updated to take account of changing circumstances".

Article 8(2) adds a labeling duty that supports training: where containers and pipes for hazardous chemical agents are not marked under the relevant EU labeling and safety sign rules, the employer must make their contents, the nature of those contents, and any associated hazards clearly identifiable.

sections.heading: How does the risk assessment decide the depth of training?

blocks.text: The risk assessment under Article 4 is the input that fixes how much training each worker needs. A low risk office cleaning task might justify a short briefing, while work with a toxic gas or a sensitizer calls for individual instruction, practical demonstration, and written procedures.

Article 4 requires the employer to determine whether hazardous chemical agents are present and to assess the risk, taking into account hazardous properties, supplier safety information, the level, type and duration of exposure, the amounts used, exposure limit values, the effect of preventive measures, and health surveillance findings. Article 4(3) requires activities such as maintenance, where significant exposure is foreseeable even after technical measures, to be included. Article 4(4) requires combined exposures to several agents to be assessed together, and Article 4(5) says a new activity involving hazardous chemical agents may only start after its risk has been assessed and the preventive measures implemented.

For training design this has a practical consequence: training for a new process must be in place before the process starts, because the preventive measures it supports must already be implemented. The assessment must be kept up to date, particularly after significant changes or when health surveillance results show it is necessary, and each such update is a trigger to review the training content.

sections.heading: What does the directive require for chemical emergencies and drills?

blocks.text: Article 7 requires the employer to set up action plans for accidents, incidents, and emergencies involving hazardous chemical agents, including "any relevant safety drills which are to be performed at regular intervals" and appropriate first aid facilities. Drills are therefore a recurring, practical element that sits alongside Article 8 training.

Article 7(2) and (3) restrict who may enter an affected area: only workers essential to repairs and other necessary work, provided with protective clothing, personal protective equipment, and specialized safety equipment that they must use while the situation persists. Unprotected persons may not remain in the area. These workers need training in the equipment and procedures before an event, not during one. Article 7 also requires information on emergency arrangements to be available to internal and external accident and emergency services.

sections.heading: Who needs which training under the directive?

blocks.text: Every worker exposed or potentially exposed to a hazardous chemical agent needs Article 8 training scaled to their risk, and some roles need more. The table below maps each obligation to the roles it applies to, the frequency, and the evidence an inspector would expect.

blocks.text: A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) that lists each hazardous agent against each role makes these assignments auditable and shows which people must be retrained when the inventory changes.

Directive (EU) 2024/869 changed the annexes of the Chemical Agents Directive, adding a binding limit value for diisocyanates and removing lead, which now sits in the carcinogens, mutagens and reprotoxic substances directive. According to [EU-OSHA's summary of Directive 98/24/EC](https://osha.europa.eu/en/legislation/directives/75), lead was removed from Annexes I and II because it is a reprotoxic substance and reprotoxic substances have been covered by Directive 2004/37/EC since 2022.

The consolidated Annex I sets a binding occupational exposure limit for diisocyanates (measured as NCO) of 6 micrograms per cubic meter over 8 hours and 12 micrograms per cubic meter short term, with skin and dermal and respiratory sensitization notations. A transitional limit of 10 micrograms per cubic meter (8 hours) and 20 micrograms per cubic meter (short term) applies until December 31, 2028. Workers handling diisocyanates need training that reflects the limit value in force and the sensitization risk, and that training must be updated when the transitional value ends.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the consolidated text of Directive 98/24/EC dated April 8, 2024 and EU-OSHA's summary, as at November 2026. Each Member State's transposing law sets the binding national limit values and may add detail, so check the national act before relying on any figure.

sections.heading: How does this directive relate to other chemical safety law?

blocks.text: The Chemical Agents Directive is the general rule, and more specific laws take priority where they are stricter. Article 1(3) applies it without prejudice to stricter provisions for carcinogens, and EU-OSHA notes the same for asbestos under Directive 2009/148/EC and for carcinogens, mutagens or reprotoxic substances under Directive 2004/37/EC, covered on [the EU Carcinogens and Mutagens Directive training page](/regulations/eu-carcinogens-and-mutagens-directive-training).

REACH and CLP feed the workplace duty: the safety data sheet and the label are the main inputs to the Article 4 assessment and to Article 8 training. A multinational that also operates in the United States will find a parallel structure in the hazard communication rule described in [OSHA hazard communication training requirements](/regulations/osha-hazard-communication-training-requirements), but the EU approach ties training depth explicitly to the employer's own risk assessment.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each hazardous agent, its controls, and its emergency actions as structured concepts linked to the risk assessment and to the roles that handle it. When a safety data sheet, limit value, or process changes, the linked concepts and the people who need updated training can be identified directly, which supports the Article 8 duty to keep information current.

faqs.q: Does the Chemical Agents Directive set a training frequency?
faqs.a: No fixed interval. Article 8 requires information and training to be updated to take account of changing circumstances, and Article 7 requires safety drills at regular intervals chosen by the employer. National transposing laws may add specific frequencies, so the Member State's act should be checked.

faqs.q: Is giving workers the safety data sheet enough?
faqs.a: No. Access to safety data sheets is only one of four Article 8 elements. Workers must also receive the risk assessment data, information on the agents and their exposure limits, and training on precautions and actions, delivered in a form that matches the level of risk.

faqs.q: Does the directive apply to chemicals produced by a process, such as welding fumes or dust?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 2(a) defines a chemical agent to include any element or compound produced, used, or released, including as waste, by any work activity, whether or not produced intentionally and whether or not placed on the market. Process generated agents must be assessed and covered by training.

faqs.q: Can chemical safety training be delivered online?
faqs.a: The directive does not prescribe a method. It says the form should vary with risk, from oral communication to individual instruction supported by written information. Higher risk tasks usually need practical, supervised instruction. See [e-learning vs instructor led compliance training](/compare/elearning-vs-instructor-led-compliance-training).
